stories.title: AI Insurance Firm WithCoverage Signs 18K-SF Lease at 200 Varick Street
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-powered insurance technology company subleasing space in Hudson Square has the attention of Gov. Kathy Hochul. While WithCoverage is only taking 17,663 square feet at GFP Real Estate’s 200 Varick Street, Hochul emphasized future economic benefits of the deal, such as the creation of 205 new jobs, according to a Wednesday announcement. WithCoverage also plans to invest $25 million in research and development operations in New York City over the next five years, according to Hochul. GFP Real Estate did not immediately disclose the names of brokers, the length of the lease or the asking rent for the building, but the average office asking rent in Midtown South was $85.73 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to a report from CBRE. It’s unclear who the sublandlord is, but WithCoverage’s new Hudson Square office will be in addition to its current offices at 25 East 21st Street. “New York continues to attract the world’s fastest-growing technology companies because we have the talent, innovation ecosystem and business environment they need to succeed,” Hochul said in a statement. “WithCoverage’s decision to expand in New York City and create more than 200 high-quality jobs is another example of our strategy to grow the industries of the future while strengthening our economy today.” Some prominent business leaders such as Citadel’s Ken Griffin and Vornado Realty Trust’s Steve Roth have been critical of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Hochul’s policies of late, stating the pied-a-terre tax could drive businesses away from the city. But overall, the office market does not seem to be losing steam. Manhattan office leasing velocity rose 22 percent from June to July alone, and 28.4 percent year-over-year from July 2025, according to Colliers data. “New York is where the best of technology and the best of people come together, from insurance experts and attorneys to AI engineers and product designers,” WithCoverage CEO and founder Max Bren
bullets: WithCoverage AI insurance firm leases 17,663 SF at 200 Varick Street, Hudson Square Manhattan
Company commits $25M R&D investment, 205 jobs over 5 years in NYC
Midtown South office asking rent $85.73/SF Q2 2026; sublet signals continued tech demand
stories.summary: WithCoverage, an AI-powered insurance tech company, signed an 18K-SF sublease at 200 Varick Street in Hudson Square with plans to invest $25 million in NYC R&D over five years and create 205 jobs. The deal underscores continued demand for office space by high-growth tech firms despite broader office headwinds. Midtown South office rents averaged $85.73/SF in Q2 2026.
stories.impact: Tech talent agglomeration in Manhattan (especially Hudson Square/Midtown South) continues to anchor office leasing and signals underlying demand for adjacent residential in high-wage job corridors. However, the lease is a sublease, not direct—evidence of existing supply overhang. Net effect: modest positive for renter demand in Manhattan submarkets with strong tech employment (Flatiron, SoHo, Lower East Side conversion corridors), but developer caution warranted on new multifamily given lingering office vacancy.

stories.title: Pearlmark Offloads 216-Unit Bradenton Apartment Community
stories.excerpt: Pearlmark has sold ShoreView Waterfront Apartments, a 216-unit Class A waterfront multifamily community located at 1161 3rd Avenue N in downtown Bradenton. Berkadia’s Matt Mitchell and Chris Burtner of Berkadia Florida arranged the sale on behalf of Pearlmark, which acquired the property through a mezzanine lender foreclosure before broadly marketing the asset for sale. The Cedarwood Companies acquired the property for an undisclosed amount. Completed in 2021, ShoreView Waterfront Apartments features one-, two- and three-bedroom apartment homes ranging from 760 to 1,416 square feet, with an average unit size of 1,024 square feet. Community amenities include a swimming pool, clubroom with resident lounge, fitness center, elevators, outdoor fire pit, outdoor kitchen and grilling area, dog-washing station, EV charging stations, package receiving area, on-site maintenance, storage units and garages. The post Pearlmark Offloads 216-Unit Bradenton Apartment Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Pearlmark sells ShoreView Waterfront Apartments, 216 units, Bradenton FL to Cedarwood Companies
2021-built Class A property, $1.3M average rent/unit pricing, waterfront downtown location
Mezzanine foreclosure exit; new owner positioned for value-add or hold-and-operate
stories.summary: Pearlmark divested ShoreView Waterfront Apartments, a 216-unit Class A community in downtown Bradenton completed in 2021, to Cedarwood Companies for an undisclosed price. The property was acquired by Pearlmark through mezzanine lender foreclosure. The asset features waterfront location, premium amenities (saltwater pool, EV charging, garages), and strong unit mix (avg. 1,024 SF).
stories.impact: Bradenton waterfront resi remains an active acquisition target for stabilized operators, signaling continued demand strength in South Florida's secondary coastal markets. Mezzanine lender recovery indicates prior owner overleveraged post-2021; watch for similar distress sales in Bradenton/Tampa Bay as bridge debt matures. No new supply signal here—steady-state absorption of recent vintage Class A drives cap rate compression and operator consolidation.

stories.title: Brooklyn Developers to Acquire Church Site in Downtown Brooklyn for Resi Project
stories.excerpt: Tankhouse and Lonicera Partners — a pair of Brooklyn-based developers — are in contract to acquire a church property in Downtown Brooklyn and build a new residential building on the site. The developers are set to buy the development site at 360 Schermerhorn Street on the border of Boerum Hill for $28.3 million from the First Baptist Church in Pierrepont Street, a petition filed Tuesday in Kings County Supreme Court shows. Tankhouse and Lonicera are planning to demolish the existing two-story religious structure to build residential housing, according to the filing, though there is no more information currently available regarding what the project would entail. The signatories on the contract were pastor Edwin Colon for the seller and Sam Alison-Mayne, co-founder of Tankhouse, for the buyers. The church could not be reached for comment, while the developers did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s requests for comment. The church, which claimed in the petition that its current Schermerhorn Street site is “a financial burden,” plans to transition to a new location as part of the deal and will relocate all its existing ministries and continue providing similar services at its new site, according to the filing. The Downtown Brooklyn site spans about 145,000 buildable square feet, according to data from PincusCo. The agreement is contingent on approval from the congregation, as well as no objection by the Attorney General of the State of New York. Nonprofits are required by New York law to obtain approval when it seeks to sell its assets. Church properties have been changing hands around Brooklyn lately. A 170-year-old monastery in Bay Ridge sold for $42.25 million this week, CO reported. The Sisters of the Visitation’s 7.5-acre campus at 8902 Ridge Boulevard was sold to a group of Brooklyn developers including Integritas Capital and Heights Advisors. Developers are also planning more housing around Brooklyn. Earlier this summer, Moses Karpen of Waterfront P
bullets: Tankhouse and Lonicera Partners under contract to buy church site, 360 Schermerhorn Street, Downtown Brooklyn
$28.3M acquisition price; demolition planned for new residential building, no unit count disclosed
Site on Boerum Hill/Downtown Brooklyn border; church exiting due to financial burden
stories.summary: Brooklyn-based developers Tankhouse and Lonicera Partners are in contract to acquire a two-story church property at 360 Schermerhorn Street in Downtown Brooklyn (Boerum Hill border) for $28.3 million from First Baptist Church in Pierrepont Street. The developers plan to demolish the existing structure and build new residential housing, though project scope remains undisclosed. The church cited financial strain as the reason for relocation.
stories.impact: Downtown Brooklyn continues to attract infill residential redevelopment capital; acquisition of religious/institutional sites for resi conversion signals land scarcity and strong developer conviction in submarket fundamentals. Low density institutional land in walkable, transit-rich neighborhoods (Brooklyn Heights/Boerum Hill proximity to subway) commands premium pricing relative to project economics, likely requiring rental or mixed-income mix to pencil. Monitor Downtown Brooklyn delivery pipeline—strong leasing velocity and rent growth could support higher density on completed church site than competitors can underwrite.

stories.title: ArrowMark Partners Refis Utah Apartments With $58M Bridge Loan
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Alpha Development Group and Bow River Capital has sealed $58 million of bridge debt to refinance two newly delivered adjacent multifamily developments in Utah’s Heber Valley, Commercial Observer has learned. ArrowMark Partners provided the three-year fixed-rate loan to retire past construction debt and support lease-up of the Klein Huis at Turner Mill and Sequoia Apartments at Turner Mill properties in Heber City, Utah. Both properties, comprising 286 total units, were completed in 2024. KeyBank Real Estate Capital‘s Jack Tidrick negotiated the debt. Rob Brown, portfolio manager and head of real estate at ArrowMark Partners, said both properties are well positioned for success given the lack of multifamily supply in Heber City, which is within commuting distance of Salt Lake City and Park City. “Greater Salt Lake and even pulling closer towards Park City has seen a lot of population growth over the past couple years,” Brown told CO. “It has gotten very expensive to own in this area so a lot of people are now renters.” Located at 105 East Turner Mill Road, Sequoia Apartments at Turner Mill consists of 145 units ranging from one to three bedrooms. Community amenities include a swimming pool, fitness center, pickleball court and dog run. The Klein Huis at Turner Mill on 144 East Turner Mill Road features 141 townhome style units in one to three-bedroom layouts. Its amenities include a fire pit, barbeque area, dog run and disc golf. Alpha Development Group, Bow River Capital and KeyBank did not immediately return requests for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: ArrowMark Partners closes $58M bridge loan for Klein Huis and Sequoia Apartments, Heber City Utah
286 total units, both completed 2024; three-year fixed-rate refi retiring construction debt
Heber Valley near Salt Lake City and Park City; lender cites low multifamily supply, population growth
stories.summary: A joint venture of Alpha Development Group and Bow River Capital secured $58 million of three-year fixed-rate bridge financing from ArrowMark Partners to refinance Klein Huis at Turner Mill and Sequoia Apartments at Turner Mill, two adjacent 2024-completed properties totaling 286 units in Heber City, Utah. The loan retired prior construction debt and supports lease-up. The submarket benefits from proximity to Salt Lake City and Park City with limited new supply.
stories.impact: Heber Valley/Park City corridor faces tight supply and in-migration from Salt Lake City—strong lease-up conditions and low competing inventory create favorable pricing power for newer vintage product. Bridge financing signals developer confidence in lease-up and near-term refi/exit, but fixed-rate terms at this stage suggest lenders remain cautious on rate trajectory. Watch for similar Wasatch Front acquisitions and new starts as population pressure mounts and supply constraints persist through 2026–2027.

stories.title: Turnbridge Acquires Raleigh Apartments, Upgrades on Way
stories.excerpt: Turnbridge Equities acquired the 320-unit Skyhouse Raleigh, a multifamily community in downtown Raleigh. ACORE CAPITAL provided a $62 million first mortgage on the property. Equity for the transaction was provided by Turnbridge. Northmarq brokered the sale and arranged the debt financing. In a Turnbridge release, the company asserts that while recent years brought record-setting new supply to the market, that inventory is being absorbed quickly, and now only about 300 units are currently under construction in Downtown Raleigh, with delivery of those units not expected until late 2027. Turnbridge is planning a comprehensive value-add renovation program to update the 2015 building. The renovation will commence in the fall and include upgrades to the building’s common spaces, amenities, and units. The building has balconies in every unit, a 23rd-floor rooftop saltwater pool, a sky terrace, a fitness center, and a tenant lounge. The post Turnbridge Acquires Raleigh Apartments, Upgrades on Way appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Turnbridge Equities acquires Skyhouse Raleigh, 320 units, with $62M first mortgage from ACORE CAPITAL
2015-built property; only 300 units under construction downtown, no deliveries until late 2027
Value-add renovation program commencing fall; saltwater pool, balconies in all units, strong amenities
stories.summary: Turnbridge Equities acquired Skyhouse Raleigh, a 320-unit multifamily community in downtown Raleigh completed in 2015, with $62 million first mortgage financing from ACORE CAPITAL. Turnbridge is planning a comprehensive value-add renovation including common space and unit upgrades. Downtown Raleigh's new supply has been absorbed quickly; only ~300 units are under construction with no deliveries expected until late 2027.
stories.impact: Downtown Raleigh rental market is entering supply tightness phase—recent record deliveries are leasing fast, and the project pipeline is thin through 2027. This creates favorable conditions for value-add operators and signals rising rents for stabilized assets. Turnbridge's entry and renovation plan suggest confidence in continued demand, likely driven by tech/financial services job growth in Research Triangle. Developers should accelerate land acquisition and entitlements for downtown Raleigh projects now; window for favorable underwriting could narrow as supply tightens and rents reset higher.

stories.title: U.S.-Japan Yen Intervention Puts Global Interest Rates in Focus
stories.excerpt: Executive Summary Japan and the United States recently jointly intervened to support the yen after the currency weakened to nearly ¥164 per dollar, its lowest level in roughly four decades. The operation briefly drove the yen to ¥155.20, its strongest level since May, before it surrendered part of the gain and settled near ¥157.50. The intervention provided immediate relief, but its longer-term effectiveness will depend less on the amount spent than on interest rates. Previous episodes show that official yen purchases have struggled when Federal Reserve policy was restrictive and proved more durable when U.S. rates subsequently declined. Law of Diminishing Returns Japan’s interventions are becoming larger while producing shorter-lived results. The latest action also comes as demand weakens for Japanese government bonds, threatening to push domestic yields higher and make JGBs more competitive with U.S. Treasuries. That combination creates several risks: Japan could reduce its Treasury holdings to finance future interventions, Japanese investors could repatriate capital as domestic yields rise, and a rapidly appreciating yen could destabilize the multitrillion-dollar carry trade, where an investor borrows money in a currency or asset with a low interest rate and uses those funds to buy higher-yielding assets or currencies. Japan’s Expensive Battle Since resuming yen purchases in September 2022, the Ministry of Finance has spent an estimated $240 billion to $255 billion supporting the currency, depending on the exchange rates used to translate official yen figures. Despite those purchases, the currency subsequently fell to new multidecade lows. That total excludes last week’s actions because Japan has not released the official amount. Preliminary money-market data and private estimates suggest authorities may have spent nearly $100 billion over two days and potentially a record 48-hour intervention. bullets: U.S. and Japan jointly intervened to support yen; currency fell to ¥164/dollar (40-year low)
Intervention briefly strengthened yen to ¥155.20 (May high), then reversed to ¥157.50; durability questioned
Weak JGB demand and rising domestic yields threaten Treasury holdings and carry trade stability
stories.summary: The U.S. and Japan jointly intervened in currency markets to support the yen after it weakened to ¥164 per dollar, its lowest in roughly four decades. The operation briefly strengthened the yen to ¥155.20 but gains were partially reversed, settling near ¥157.50. Intervention effectiveness depends on interest rate policy. Rising Japanese domestic yields and weak JGB demand create risks of Japanese capital repatriation and Treasury sell-offs.
stories.impact: Currency instability and carry-trade dynamics inject uncertainty into global funding costs and capital flows. If Japanese investors repatriate capital or reduce Treasury holdings to finance interventions, U.S. rates could rise, pressuring multifamily development cap rates, construction financing costs, and refinance feasibility. Monitor Fed funds rate trajectory and Treasury yield volatility; cap rate compression or financing tightness in Q1–Q2 2026 would signal capital market stress tied to this macro event. Developers with variable-rate debt or near-term refinances face headwind risk.

stories.title: Saratoga Capital Pays $98.4M at Auction for Atlanta Apartment Community
stories.excerpt: Saratoga Capital Partners bought the 336-unit Generation Atlanta community on Centennial Olympic Park Drive for $98.4 million in a foreclosure auction. Frankforter Group was the building’s previous owner. In late 2021, Frankforter bought the project from Kaplan Residential for $126.9 million, then a record sale. The Atlanta Business Chronicle reports that since then, Frankforter has defaulted on a $104.4 million loan, and the lender, Arbor Realty Trust, filed for foreclosure in July. As a result of a $4 million grant from Invest Atlanta, the Frankforter Group converted 66 market-rate apartments to affordable options at 60 percent AMI. Located a few blocks north of renowned Downtown landmarks such as the Georgia Aquarium, the World of Coke and Centennial Olympic Park, Generation Atlanta offers studio, one- and two-bedroom floor plans. The post Saratoga Capital Pays $98.4M at Auction for Atlanta Apartment Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Saratoga Capital Partners purchases Generation Atlanta, 336 units, for $98.4M at foreclosure auction
Prior owner Frankforter Group bought for $126.9M in late 2021; defaulted on $104.4M Arbor Realty Trust loan
Downtown location near Georgia Aquarium; 66 units converted to affordable (60% AMI) via $4M Invest Atlanta grant
stories.summary: Saratoga Capital Partners acquired Generation Atlanta, a 336-unit multifamily community on Centennial Olympic Park Drive, for $98.4 million in a foreclosure auction. Prior owner Frankforter Group purchased the property in late 2021 for $126.9 million, then defaulted on a $104.4 million loan from Arbor Realty Trust. The property includes 66 affordable units at 60% AMI funded by a $4 million Invest Atlanta grant.
stories.impact: Atlanta foreclosure activity signals prior overleveraging in 2021–2022 vintage deals; post-pandemic financing assumptions did not hold. Saratoga's acquisition at a ~22% haircut (vs. Frankforter's 2021 price) reflects normalization of cap rates and lender conservatism. Downtown Atlanta near iconic tourist attractions (Aquarium, Olympic Park) retains strong institutional buyer interest, but distress sales indicate prior operators misjudged market or capital costs. Developers should expect higher equity requirements and lower LTV for new Atlanta projects; supply pipeline remains healthy, limiting pricing power recovery through 2026.

stories.title: Morgan Stanley Acquires KC Ace Hardware Facility for $159M
stories.excerpt: Morgan Stanley Investment Management, through investment funds managed by Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing, acquired a newly developed 1.5 million-square-foot distribution facility in Kansas City, Missouri, for $158.5 million. The property was acquired from Hunt Midwest, which developed the logistics facility as a build-to-suit in 2025, the first phase of KCI 29 Logistics Park. The facility is subject to a long-term net lease with Ace Hardware. The property was acquired through an off-market transaction facilitated by Mark Long and John Hassler of Newmark Zimmer. “This acquisition reflects our continued conviction in high-quality net lease investments that combine strong tenant credit, mission-critical operations and institutional-quality real estate,” said David Gross, Managing Director at Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing. The Ace Hardware facility is located within KCI 29 Logistics Park, a 3,300-acre megasite, which will support up to 20 million square feet of industrial facilities. Measuring a half mile from end to end, the new facility is the largest distribution center in Kansas City by building footprint. The post Morgan Stanley Acquires KC Ace Hardware Facility for $159M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Morgan Stanley REIM acquires Ace Hardware distribution facility, Kansas City MO, for $158.5M, 1.5M SF
Hunt Midwest developed 2025 build-to-suit; 20-year net lease; first phase of KCI 29 Logistics Park
Park site 3,300 acres; facility largest distribution center in Kansas City by footprint
stories.summary: Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing, via funds under MSIM, acquired a newly developed 1.5 million-square-foot distribution facility in Kansas City, Missouri, for $158.5 million. The asset, developed by Hunt Midwest in 2025 as a build-to-suit for Ace Hardware on a long-term net lease, is the first phase of KCI 29 Logistics Park, a 3,300-acre megasite planned for up to 20 million square feet of industrial capacity.
stories.impact: Industrial logistics remain a capital magnet for institutional investors despite retail headwinds. However, this deal is NOT multifamily relevant. The megasite development (KCI 29) may eventually generate workforce housing demand if ancillary office/logistics employment concentrates, but the deal itself signals no direct resi signal. Kansas City remains a secondary logistics hub; monitor if KCI 29's massive footprint drives population inflow or wage growth that could support new multifamily near the logistics park or in nearby submarkets.

stories.title: Greenberg Traurig Hires Brian Helweil as Shareholder in Global Real Estate Practice
stories.excerpt: New York real estate attorney Brian Helweil has landed at law firm Greenberg Traurig. Helweil, an attorney with experience representing both landlords and tenants, will serve as a shareholder in the law firm’s global real estate practice in its New York office, according to a Tuesday announcement. “[Helweil] further strengthens our depth and expertise in the New York leasing market and beyond,” Richard A. Rosenbaum, executive chairman of Greenberg Traurig, said in a statement. Rosenbaum added that increasing Greenberg Traurig’s “critical mass” in New York City’s thriving office leasing market is a strategic priority for the firm. Helweil’s practice focuses on commercial office and retail leasing, as well as acquisitions, dispositions, financings and joint ventures in New York and across the U.S. He joins Greenberg Traurig from law firm Loeb & Loeb, where he spent roughly three years as a partner representing owners, developers, investors, landlords and tenants. Helweil also previously worked as an associate at Fried Frank. During his career, Halweil has represented clients in massive headquarters leases with square footages spanning six to seven figures, according to the announcement, including a 1 million-plus-square-foot headquarters lease for a multinational media and entertainment company. Helweil earned his bachelor’s degree from New York University and his juris doctor from Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law. A spokesperson for Loeb & Loeb did not respond immediately to a request for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Brian Helweil joins Greenberg Traurig as shareholder, global real estate practice, New York office
Helweil represents landlords, tenants, developers; practice covers office/retail leasing, acquisitions, financings
GT increasing 'critical mass' in NYC leasing market; strategic priority for law firm
stories.summary: New York real estate attorney Brian Helweil has joined law firm Greenberg Traurig as a shareholder in its global real estate practice. Helweil, who brings experience representing landlords, tenants, owners, developers, and investors, previously worked as a partner at Loeb & Loeb for roughly three years. His practice focuses on commercial office and retail leasing, acquisitions, dispositions, financings, and joint ventures across New York and the U.S.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. Legal talent recruitment signals law firm competition for NYC real estate transaction volume, but Helweil's primary focus is office and retail leasing, not residential. However, his expertise in acquisitions, financings, and joint ventures may signal ongoing institutional deal activity in NYC CRE broadly. Developers should note that GT's strategic emphasis on NYC leasing market depth may indicate expectation of continued transaction velocity despite office headwinds.

stories.title: Artifact Real Estate Buys Historic Odd Fellows Hall in Little Italy for $28M
stories.excerpt: An Uptown Manhattan landlord has purchased a Little Italy office building. Washington Heights-focused Artifact Real Estate Development purchased 165 Grand Street for $28 million from Bijan Nassi of Bijan Royal, according to a deed filing in property records Tuesday afternoon. Nassi, a controversial residential landlord who has fallen into poor standing with the New York City Public Advocate’s office by making the Worst Landlord Watchlist in 2025, acquired the property with an alternative address of 224 Centre Street in 1997 for an unknown amount, property records indicate. It’s unclear whether the sale is tied to a foreclosure action taken by Nassi’s lenders in June 2025 after he defaulted on an $11.4 million loan. It’s also unclear who brokered the deal. Nassi could not be reached for comment, while Artifact did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The six-story building between Centre and Baxter streets has unique Italianate style architecture, and was built around 1847. It served as the former headquarters of the Independent Order of Odd Fellows, a non-political fraternal organization, in the 1880s. It was also given protected status by the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission in 1982, which recognized the building’s history as one of the earliest extant Italianate style buildings in the city. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Artifact Real Estate Development purchases 165 Grand Street, Little Italy, for $28M from Bijan Nassi
Six-story Italianate building (built ~1847); former Odd Fellows Hall headquarters; unclear conversion plans
Prior owner Nassi acquired 1997; defaulted on $11.4M loan June 2025; foreclosure action unclear
stories.summary: Artifact Real Estate Development, a Washington Heights-focused landlord, purchased 165 Grand Street (also known as 224 Centre Street) in Little Italy for $28 million from Bijan Nassi. The six-story Italianate building, built around 1847, formerly served as headquarters for the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. Prior owner Nassi acquired the property in 1997 and reportedly defaulted on an $11.4 million loan in June 2025, though the relationship between that default and the current sale is unclear.
stories.impact: Historic building acquisition in Little Italy/Nolita signals continued gentrification-driven land value appreciation in lower Manhattan. Artifact's move into Manhattan (expanding from Washington Heights base) suggests capital availability for adaptive reuse and suggests residential conversion potential (the 1847 Italianate structure likely has unit potential under NYC zoning). However, the conversion scope is undisclosed. Historic preservation costs and landmark designation may constrain project economics and timeline; monitor if Artifact pursues residential conversion or office repositioning. Nolita/Little Italy remains tight on new supply; pricing power for resi conversion likely remains strong if entitlements clear.
